¶
'''bitchery†''' (bich′e̤-ri), ''n.'' [< ''bitch'' + ''-ery.''] Vileness or coarseness in a woman; unchastity or lewdness in general.

'''bitch-wood''' (bich′wu̇d), ''n.'' The wood of a leguminous tree, ''Lonchocarpus latifolius,'' of the West Indies and tropical South America.

'''bite''' (bīt), ''v.''; pret. ''bit'', pp. ''bitten'', sometimes ''bit'', ppr. ''biting''. [< ME. ''biten'' (pret. ''bot'', ''boot'', pl. ''biten'', pp. ''biten''), < AS. ''bītan'' (pret. ''bāt'', pl. ''biton'', pp. ''biten'') = OS. ''bītan'' = OFries. ''bīta'' = D. ''bijten'' = MLG. ''bīten'', LG. ''biten'' = OHG. ''bīzan'', MHG. ''bīzen'', G. ''beissen'' = Icel. ''bīta'' = Sw. ''bita'' = Dan. ''bide'' = Goth. ''beitan'', bite, = L. ''findere'' (√ *''fid''), cleave, = Skt. √ ''bhid'', divide. From the AS. come ''bite'', ''n.'', ''bit''<sup>1</sup>, ''bit''<sup>2</sup>, ''bitter''<sup>1</sup>, ''beetle''<sup>2</sup>, ''beetle''<sup>3</sup>; to the Icel. are due ''bait''<sup>1</sup>, and prob. ''bitt''; from L. ''findere'' come ''fissile'', ''fissure'', ''bifid'', etc.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To cut, pierce, or divide with the teeth: as, to ''bite'' an apple.
{{smaller block|The fish that once was caught new bait wil hardly ''byte.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. i. 4.}}}}
'''2.''' To remove with the teeth; cut away by biting: with ''off'', ''out'', etc.: as, to ''bite off'' a piece of an apple, or ''bite'' a piece ''out'' of it; to ''bite off'' one’s nose to spite one’s face.
{{smaller block|I’ll ''bite'' my tongue ''out'', ere it prove a traitor.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Wit at Several Weapons, iv. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' To grasp or grip with the teeth; press the teeth strongly upon: as, to ''bite'' the thumb or lip. (See phrases below.)
{{smaller block|There Faction roar, Rebellion ''bite'' her chain.
{{right|''Pope'', Windsor Forest, l. 421.}}}}

2. One who cheats or defrauds; also, formerly, one who deceives by way of joke.
{{smaller block|A ''biter'' is one who tells you a thing you have no reason to disbelieve in itself, and, if you give him credit, laughs in your face, and triumphs that he has deceived you.
{{right|''Spectator'', No. 504.}}}}

'''biterminal''' (bī-tėr′mi-nal), ''n.'' [Tr. of Gr. ἐκ δύο ὀνομάτων.] A binomial line; a line that is the sum of two incommensurable lines.

'''biternate''' (bī-tėr′nāt), ''a.'' [< ''bi-''<sup>2</sup> + ''ternate.''] In ''bot.'', doubly ternate, as when each of the partial petioles of a ternate leaf bears three leaflets.

'''bite-sheep†''' (bīt′shēp), ''n.'' [So MLG. ''biteschāp'', G. ''biss-schaf'', with the same allusion.] A once favorite pun upon ''bishop'', as if one who bites the sheep which he ought to feed. ''N. E. D.''

'''bitheism''' (bī′thē-izm), ''n.'' [< ''bi-''<sup>2</sup> + ''theism.''] Belief in two gods, specifically a good and an evil one; dualism. [Rare.]

'''biti''' (bē′tē), ''n.'' [E. Ind.] An East Indian name for species of ''Dalbergia'', especially ''D. latifolia'', one of the East Indian rosewoods.

'''biting''' (bī′ting), ''n.'' [< ME. ''biting''; verbal n. of ''bite'', ''v.''] '''1.''' The action of cutting, piercing, etc., in any sense of ''bite''.—'''2.''' The corroding action of a mordant upon a metal plate, wherever the lines of a design, drawn upon a prepared ground, have been laid bare with a needle, as in etching, or the surface is alternately stopped out and exposed, as in aquatint.

'''biting''' (bī′ting), ''p. a.'' [Ppr. of ''bite'', ''v.''] '''1.''' Nipping; keen: as, ''biting'' cold; ''biting'' weather.
{{smaller block|<poem>The western breeze,
And years of ''biting'' frost and ''biting'' rain,</poem>}}

{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 325.}}}}
'''2.''' Severe; sharp; bitter; painful: as, a “''biting'' affliction,” ''Shak.'', M. W. of W., v. 5.—'''3.''' Acrid; hot; pungent: as, a ''biting'' taste. Hence —'''4.''' Sharp; severe; cutting; sarcastic: as, a ''biting'' remark.
{{smaller block|This was a nipping sermon, a pinching sermon, a ''biting'' sermon.
{{right|''Latimer'', Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1550.}}
Pope’s provocation was too often the mere opportunity to say a ''biting'' thing, where he could do it safely.
{{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 1st ser., p. 70.}}}}

'''biting-dragon''' (bī′ting-drag″ọn), ''n.'' An old name for tarragon, ''Artemisia Dracunculus.''

'''bitingly''' (bī′ting-li), ''adv.'' In a biting manner; sarcastically; sneeringly.

'''bitingness''' (bī′ting-nes), ''n.'' Pungency; acridity.

'''bit-key''' (bit′kē), ''n.'' A key designed to fit a permutation-lock, the steps of which are formed by movable bits. See ''lock.''

'''bitless''' (bit′les), ''a.'' [< ''bit''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', + ''-less.''] Without bit or bridle.
{{smaller block|''Bitless'' Numidian horse.{{right|''Fanshawe'', Æneid, iv.}}}}

'''bitling†''' (bit′ling), ''n.'' [< ''bit''<sup>2</sup> + dim. ''-ling.''] A very small bit or piece.

'''bitmouth†''' (bit′mouth), ''n.'' The bit or iron put into a horse’s mouth. ''Bailey.''

'''bitnoben''' (bit-nō′ben), ''n.'' [A corruption of the Hind. name ''bit lavan'', or ''bid lavan'': ''bit'', ''bid'' (cerebral ''t'' or ''d'') is of uncertain meaning; ''lavan'', dial. ''laban'', ''lon'', ''lun'', etc., < Skt. ''lavana'', salt.] A

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|bit|567|bitnoben}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|Your case is not a ''bit'' clearer than it was seven years ago.
{{right|''Arbuthnot.''}}}}
{{smaller block|My young companion was a ''bit'' of a poet, a ''bit'' of an artist, a ''bit'' of a musician, and . . . a ''bit'' of an actor.
{{right|''T. Hook'', Gilbert Gurney, I. i.}}}}
'''5.''' Crisis; nick of time. [Scotch.]—'''6.''' A small piece of ground; a spot. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|It’s a bieldy enough ''bit.'' {{right|''Scott'', Waverley, II. xxiii.}}}}
'''7.''' Any small coin: as, a fourpenny-''bit;'' a sixpenny-''bit.'' {{smaller|Specifically, the name of a small West Indian coin worth about 10 cents; also, in parts of the United States, of a silver coin formerly current (in some States called a ''Mexican shilling''), of the value of 12½ cents; now, chiefly in the West, the sum of 12½ cents.}}
{{smaller block|With six ''bits'' in his pocket and an axe upon his shoulder.
{{right|''The Century'', XXVII. 29.}}}}
'''A bit of blood.''' {{smaller|See ''blood.''}}—'''A long bit,''' {{smaller|fifteen cents. [Western U. S.]}}—'''A short bit,''' {{smaller|ten cents. [Western U. S.]}}—'''Bit by bit,''' {{smaller|little by little; imperceptibly.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And, ''bit by bit'',
The cunning years steal all from us but woe.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Comm. Ode.}}}}
'''To give a bit of one’s mind,''' {{smaller|to speak out frankly what one thinks of a person or a transaction; express one’s candid conviction unrestrained by reserve or delicacy: generally to the person himself, and in unflattering terms.}}
{{smaller block|He had ''given'' the house what was called ''a bit of his mind'' on the subject, and he wished very much that he would give them the whole.
{{right|''Lord Campbell'', London Times, April 12, 1864.}}}}
='''Syn. 4.''' {{smaller|Scrap, fragment, morsel, particle, atom.}}

'''bit<sup>3</sup>''' (bit). Preterit and occasional past participle of ''bite.''

'''bit<sup>4</sup>†.''' A Middle English and Anglo-Saxon contraction of ''biddeth'', third person singular indicative present of ''bid''.

'''bit<sup>5</sup>†''', ''n.'' An obsolete spelling of ''bitt''.

'''bit<sup>6</sup>†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''butt<sup>3</sup>''.

'''bitangent''' (bī-tan′jẹnt), ''n.''   [< ''bi-<sup>2</sup>'' + ''tangent.'']   In ''math.'', a double tangent; a straight line which touches a given curve at two points. {{smaller|If ''m'' denotes the degree and ''n'' the class of a curve, then (''n''—''m'') (''n'' + ''m''—9) is the excess of the number of its bitangents over the number of its double points.—'''Isolated bitangent,''' a real line tangent to a curve at two imaginary points.}} {{img float|file=century v01 p0593 c1f1.png|width=107px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Bitangent to Cassinian Oval.}}}}

'''bitangential''' (bī-tan-jen′shạl), ''a.''   [< ''bitangent'' + ''-ial.'']   In ''math.'', pertaining to a bitangent. {{smaller|—'''Bitangential curve,''' a curve which passes through the points of contact of the bitangents of a given curve.}}

'''bitartrate''' (bī-tär′trāt), ''n.''   [< ''bi-<sup>2</sup>'' + ''tartrate.'']   A tartrate which contains one hydrogen atom replaceable by a base.—{{smaller|'''Potassium bitartrate.''' Same as ''cream of tartar'', or ''argol'' (which see).}}

'''bit-brace''' (bit′brās), ''n.'' A tool for holding and turning a boring-bit; a brace; a bit-stock. {{smaller|—'''Bit-brace die,''' a small screw-cutting die used with a brace.}}

'''bitch''' (bich), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bicche'', ''biche'', < AS. ''bicce'', also ''bicge'', = Icel. ''bikkja'' = Norw. ''bikkje'', a bitch. Cf. G. ''betze'', ''petze'', a bitch, and F. ''biche'', a bitch, also a fawn. The relations of these forms are undetermined.]   '''1.''' The female of the dog; also, by extension, the female of other canine animals, as of the wolf and fox.—'''2.''' A coarse name of reproach for a woman.
{{smaller block|John had not run a-madding so long had it not been for an extravagant ''bitch'' of a wife.
{{right|''Arbuthnot'', John Bull, p. 9.}}}}

'''bitchery†''' (bich′e̤-ri), ''n.''   [< ''bitch'' + ''-ery.'']   Vileness or coarseness in a woman; unchastity or lewdness in general.

'''bitch-wood''' (bich′wu̇d), ''n.'' The wood of a leguminous tree, ''Lonchocarpus latifolius,'' of the West Indies and tropical South America.

'''bite''' (bīt), ''v.''; pret. ''bit'', pp. ''bitten'', sometimes ''bit'', ppr. ''biting''. [< ME. ''biten'' (pret. ''bot'', ''boot'', pl. ''biten'', pp. ''biten''), < AS. ''bītan'' (pret. ''bāt'', pl. ''biton'', pp. ''biten'') = OS. ''bītan'' = OFries. ''bīta'' = D. ''bijten'' = MLG. ''bīten'', LG. ''biten'' = OHG. ''bīzan'', MHG. ''bīzen'', G. ''beissen'' = Icel. ''bīta'' = Sw. ''bita'' = Dan. ''bide'' = Goth. ''beitan'', bite, = L. ''findere'' (√ *''fid''), cleave, = Skt. √ ''bhid'', divide. From the AS. come ''bite'', ''n.'', ''bit''<sup>1</sup>, ''bit''<sup>2</sup>, ''bitter''<sup>1</sup>, ''beetle''<sup>2</sup>, ''beetle''<sup>3</sup>; to the Icel. are due ''bait''<sup>1</sup>, and prob. ''bitt''; from L. ''findere'' come ''fissile'', ''fissure'', ''bifid'', etc.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To cut, pierce, or divide with the teeth: as, to ''bite'' an apple.
{{smaller block|The fish that once was caught new bait wil hardly ''byte.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. i. 4.}}}}
'''2.''' To remove with the teeth; cut away by biting: with ''off'', ''out'', etc.: as, to ''bite off'' a piece of an apple, or ''bite'' a piece ''out'' of it; to ''bite off'' one’s nose to spite one’s face.
{{smaller block|I’ll ''bite'' my tongue ''out'', ere it prove a traitor.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Wit at Several Weapons, iv. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' To grasp or grip with the teeth; press the teeth strongly upon: as, to ''bite'' the thumb or lip. (See phrases below.)
{{smaller block|There Faction roar, Rebellion ''bite'' her chain.
{{right|''Pope'', Windsor Forest, l. 421.}}}} '''4.''' To sting, as an insect: as, to be ''bitten'' by a flea.—'''5.''' To cause a sharp or smarting pain in; cause to smart: as, pepper ''bites'' the mouth.—'''6.''' To nip, as with frost; blast, blight, or injure.
{{smaller block|<poem>Like an envious sneaping frost,
That ''bites'' the first-born infants of the spring.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>All three of them are desperate; their great guilt,
Like poison given to work a great time after,
Now ’gins to ''bite'' the spirits. ''Shak.'', Tempest, iii. 3.</poem>}}
'''7.''' To take fast hold of; grip or catch into or on, so as to act with effect; get purchase from, as by friction: as, the anchor ''bites'' the ground; the file ''bites'' the iron; the wheels ''bite'' the rails.
{{smaller block|The last screw of the rack having been turned so often that its purchase crumbled, and it now turned and turned with nothing to ''bite''.
{{right|''Dickens.''}}}}
'''8.''' In ''etching'', to corrode or eat into with aquafortis or other mordant, as a metal surface that has been laid bare with an etching-needle: often with ''in'': as, the plate is now ''bitten in''.—'''9.''' To cheat; trick; deceive; overreach: now only in the past participle: as, the biter was ''bit''.
{{smaller block|The rogue was ''bit''.
{{right|''Pope'', Moral Essays, iii. 364.}}}}
{{smaller block|At last she played for her left eye; . . . this too she lost; however, she had the consolation of ''biting'' the sharper, for he never perceived that it was made of glass till it became his own.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Citizen of the World, cii.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To bite the dust''' or '''the ground,''' to fall; be thrown or struck down; be vanquished or humbled.}}
{{smaller block|His vanquished rival was to ''bite the dust'' before him.
{{right|''Disraeli.''}}}}

{{smaller block|'''To bite the glove.''' See ''glove.''—'''To bite the lip,''' to press the lip between the teeth in order to repress signs of anger, mirth, or other emotion. (Compare ''to bite the tongue.'')—'''To bite the thumb at†''', to insult or defy by putting the thumb-nail into the mouth, and with a jerk making it knack.}}
{{smaller block|I will ''bite my thumb at'' them, which is a disgrace to them, if they bear it.
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., i. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|'''To bite the tongue,''' to hold one’s tongue; repress (angry) speech; maintain fixed silence. (Compare ''to bite the lip,'' and ''to hold one’s tongue.'')}}
{{smaller block|<poem>So York must sit, and fret, and ''bite his tongue,''
While his own lands are bargain’d for and sold.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|='''Syn.''' See ''eat.''}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To have a habit of biting or snapping at persons or things: as, a dog that ''bites;'' a ''biting'' horse.—'''2.''' To pierce, sting, or inflict injury by biting, literally or figuratively.
{{smaller block|It [wine] ''biteth'' like a serpent and stingeth like an adder.
{{right|Prov. xxiii. 32.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Look, when he fawns he ''bites;'' and when he ''bites,''
His venom tooth will rankle to the death.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Smiling and careless, casting words that ''bit''
Like poisoned darts.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, II. 327.}}}}
'''3.''' To take a bait, as a fish: either literally or figuratively.
{{smaller block|Bait the hook well: this fish will ''bite.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|We’ll bait that men may ''bite'' fair.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Wildgoose Chase.}}}}
'''4.''' To take and keep hold; grip or catch into another object, so as to act on it with effect, obtain purchase or leverage-power from it, and the like: as, the anchor ''bites;'' cog-wheels ''bite'' when the teeth of one enter into the notches of the other and cause it to revolve.

{{smaller block|In dry weather the roads require to be watered before being swept, so that the brushes may ''bite''. {{right|''Mayhew.''}}}}

{{smaller|'''To bite at,''' to snap at with the teeth; hence, figuratively, to snarl or carp at; inveigh against.}}

<poem>No marvel, though you ''bite'' so sharp ''at'' reasons,
You are so empty of them.   ''Shak.'', T. and C., ii. 2.</poem>

{{smaller|'''To bite in.''' (''a'') To corrode, as the acid used in etching. (''b'') To repress one’s thoughts, or restrain one’s feelings.}}

'''bite''' (bīt), ''n.''   [< late ME. ''byte, bite'' (''bīte''), taking the place of earlier ''bite'' (''bĭte''), in mod. E. ''bit'' (see ''bit''<sup>1</sup>); from the verb.]   '''1.''' The act of cutting, piercing, or wounding with the teeth or as with the teeth: as, the ''bite'' of a dog; the ''bite'' of a crab.—'''2.''' The seizing of bait by a fish: as, waiting for a ''bite''.

{{smaller block|I have known a very good fisher angle diligently four or six hours for a river carp, and not have a ''bite''. {{right|''I. Walton'', Complete Angler.}}}}

'''3.''' A wound made by the teeth of an animal or by any of the biting, piercing, or stinging organs of the lower animals: as, a dog’s ''bite;'' a mosquito-''bite;'' a flea-''bite''.

{{smaller block|Their venom’d ''bite''.
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Virgil’s Georgics.}}}}

'''4.''' As much as is taken at once by biting; a mouthful: as, a ''bite'' of bread.

<poem>Better one ''bite'' at forty, of Truth’s bitter rind,
Than the hot wine that gushed from the vintage of twenty!</poem>{{right|''Lowell'', Life of Blondel.}}

'''5.''' Food; victuals: as, three days without either ''bite'' or sup.—'''6.''' The catch or hold that one object or one part of a mechanical apparatus has on another; specifically, in a file, the roughness or power of abrasion: as, the ''bite'' of an anchor on the ground; the ''bite'' of the wheels of a locomotive on the rails.
{{smaller block|The shorter the ''bite'' of a crowbar, the greater is the power gained.
{{right|''W. Matthews'', Getting on in the World, p. 119.}}}}
'''7.''' In ''etching'', the corrosion effected by the acid. —'''8.''' In ''printing'', an imperfection in a printed sheet caused by part of the impression being received on the frisket or paper mask.—'''9†.''' A cheat; a trick; a fraud.
{{smaller block|I’ll teach you a way to outwit Mrs. Johnson; it is a new-fangled way of being witty, and they call it a ''bite''.
{{right|''Swift'', To a Friend of Mrs. Johnson, 1703.}}}}
'''10†.''' A sharper; one who cheats.   ''Johnson''.—'''His bark is worse than his bite.''' {{smaller|See ''bark''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''biteless''' (bīt′les), ''a.''   [< ''bite'', ''n.'', + ''-less''.]   Without bite; wanting in ability or desire to bite; harmless.
{{smaller block|Chilled them [midges] speechless and ''biteless''.
{{right|''The Century'', XXVII. 780.}}}}

'''bitentaculate''' (bī-ten-tak′ụ̄-lāt), ''a.''   [< ''bi-''<sup>2</sup> + ''tentaculate''.]   Having two tentacles, or a pair of organs likened to tentacles.
{{smaller block|The gonophore contained in a gonangium, somewhat like that of Laomedea, is set free as a ciliated ''bitentaculate'' body.
{{right|''Huxley'', Anat. Invert., p. 120.}}}}

'''biter''' (bī′tėr), ''n.''   [ME. ''biter'', ''bitere''; < ''bite'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' One who or that which bites; an animal given to biting; a fish apt to take bait.
{{smaller block|Great barkers are no ''biters''.
{{right|''Camden''.}}}}
{{smaller block|A bold ''biter''.
{{right|''I. Walton'', Complete Angler.}}}} 2. One who cheats or defrauds; also, formerly, one who deceives by way of joke.
{{smaller block|A ''biter'' is one who tells you a thing you have no reason to disbelieve in itself, and, if you give him credit, laughs in your face, and triumphs that he has deceived you.
{{right|''Spectator'', No. 504.}}}}
